title: The Chinese and Greek painters
hook: one team paints a wall, the other only polishes theirs until it mirrors everything (Masnavi 1.3467ff)
tomorrow: of course there are rude people

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three fish, and the one that left before the net came. Leave in time.

Some people fill a room. They've got the stories, the opinions, the funny voices, and they're great company. And then there's the other kind: the friend you tell something to, and somehow, when they listen, you see your own life more clearly. They don't add much. They reflect. You leave feeling more like yourself. Both are gifts. But Rumi tells a story about a contest between the two, a painting contest judged by a king. One team brings a hundred colors. The other brings none at all.
screen: `SOME PEOPLE FILL A ROOM.` → `SOME PEOPLE REFLECT.` → `THE CHINESE AND GREEK PAINTERS.`

segments.voice: It's in Book One of the Masnavi. The Chinese painters say: we're the better artists. The Greeks, by which Rumi means the painters of the Byzantine lands, say: no, we are. So the king sets a test. Each team gets a room, facing each other, with a curtain hung between. The Chinese ask the king for a hundred colors, and every morning they collect more paint from his treasury. The Greeks say: no colors are right for our work. All we do is remove the rust. They shut their door and polish, day after day, until the wall is as clear and bright as the sky. The Chinese finish first, and beat drums for joy. The king comes in and is amazed by their painting. Then he goes to the Greeks, and they pull back the curtain. All the Chinese pictures, reflected in that polished wall, shine back even more beautifully than on the wall where they were painted. Rumi tells us who the Greeks are: the Sufis, he says, who don't rely on study and books and learning, but have polished their hearts clean of greed, envy and malice. A heart polished like that is a mirror. It can receive every image, without end. Rumi isn't saying here that learning is useless. He's saying the heart's work isn't adding more, it's clearing away, and a clear heart takes in the whole world. Your line: polish the mirror.
screen: `A CONTEST BEFORE THE KING.` · `A HUNDRED COLORS, OR NONE.` · `THE POLISHED WALL SHINES BRIGHTER.` · then, large: `POLISH THE MIRROR.`

segments.voice: Picture a mirror inside you, a little dusty from the week. With each out-breath, imagine one layer of dust coming off: a worry, a grudge, an old comparison. Don't add anything; just clear, slowly, the way you'd clean a window or a table.
Mirror. One team paints with a hundred colors; the other only polishes its wall, until it reflects everything more beautifully, like a heart cleared of greed and envy. Today's word.
Your line: polish the mirror. A clear heart takes in everything. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 211 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: OF COURSE THERE ARE RUDE PEOPLE.`

howItsDone: Sufi teachers speak of polishing the heart, and some describe dhikr, the remembrance of God, as the polish that clears it.

fork.setup: you're one of the Greek painters. the other team has a hundred colors. what do you ask the king for?
fork.reveal: they asked for no colors at all. they polished their wall until it reflected everything.

original.note: Persian: a mirror. for Rumi, the polished heart.

trapdoor: what you thought: a contest about who paints better.
what it means: the heart's work isn't adding more but clearing away, until it reflects everything.
what a scholar hears: the Sufi image of the heart as a mirror polished of rust, found before Rumi in al-Ghazali, who tells a version of this same painters' contest.

a picture of vanity and too much self-regard
a magic glass that shows you the future

the whole hive, a community working as one

notes: Paraphrased from Nicholson: the claim of each side, the king's test, facing rooms and curtain, a hundred colors from the treasury, 'our work is only to remove the rust', drums, the reflection, the Greeks as Sufis without study and books who have polished their breasts of greed, cupidity and malice. Confirm each.
'Greeks' (Rumi's Rumiyan): the script glosses as 'painters of the Byzantine lands'. Confirm.
Al-Ghazali's earlier version of the painters' contest (Ihya, Book of the Marvels of the Heart): confirm reference; in his version the parties may be named differently.
Story contains a contest between two peoples; the script keeps it as Rumi's parable and does not rank peoples.
